title: The full trail on contracts, grants and leases
question: Where a Board file about a contract, lease or other money matter names a lobbying client as the other party: did the client’s lobbyists contact the sponsor, and did the client’s circle give to the sponsor beforehand?
finding: 136 passed Board files about a contract, lease, agreement or other money matter name as counterparty a client that was paying a lobbyist around that time; 49 of them name a sponsor (the rest came from departments with none). In 13 the client’s lobbyists had reported contacting the sponsor in the three years before passage, in 8 the client’s circle had given to the sponsor’s committees, and in 2 both. All four links (fees paid, contact with the sponsor, giving to the sponsor, sponsorship of a file with a dollar amount) are present in 1 sponsor-and-client pair covering 1 file, with $1,000 of giving beside $10.0 million stated in the file. Supervisors the circle had given to were sponsors in 23.8% of 21 cases against 8.8% of 411 for other sitting supervisors (a gap beyond chance: 5 against 1.5 expected when the giving is shuffled among the supervisors sitting for each file). A final Board roll call is on disk for 126 of the 136 files (7 of them read from the Clerk’s minutes; 10 of the others passed before 2015): 117 passed with no vote against and 9 were divided. In the rows below, a sponsor who was on that roll call voted aye in 17 of 17 cases, no in 0, and was excused or absent in 0; in 4 more the sponsor was not on the roll call (4 of them files whose sponsor of record is “Mayor”). 38 more files are gifts or grants a lobbying client made to the City; they are listed but not counted. 2 of the 17 budget add-backs that name an organization name a lobbying client.
how: The Board’s money files (contracts, grants, leases, loans, settlements and gifts to the City, with the counterparty and amount read from each title) are matched by name to lobbying clients active within two years of the file’s introduction. For each sponsor: the client’s payments to its lobbyists in the two years before introduction through passage; contacts by the client’s lobbyists with the sponsor in the three years before passage; and contributions from the client, its officers, its lobbyists and their firms to the sponsor’s committees from two years before introduction to passage. “Mayor” as sponsor is resolved as in the measures screen. The chance test compares supervisors sitting at introduction, file by file. Add-back rows come from the site’s “Earmarks, bids and other public bodies” page, with the district’s supervisor that June taken from the roll calls. City payments afterwards are the three fiscal years after passage. The final vote is the Board’s last roll call on the measure itself, read from the Board’s roll-call pages for money files (2015 to November 2026): the tally, the members voting no, and the sponsor’s own vote on that roll call. A file passed before 2015 has no roll call to show. Where the vote page lists no member the votes are taken from the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and the row says so. The divided votes are set out member by member in the screen on divided votes, and whether members the circle had given to voted differently from their colleagues is tested in the screen on votes.
limits: Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. An official can sponsor or vote for something a donor wants because the official already favoured it; a donor can give to an official because of what the official already stands for. Most contracts and leases reach the Board from a department after a competition the sponsor took no part in; the sponsor is often the district’s supervisor or the Mayor carrying a routine file, and the Board’s vote is usually unanimous (117 of the 126 roll calls here had no vote against), so a sponsor’s aye says nothing by itself. A supervisor sponsors files about their own district and interests, and the businesses and institutions there are the ones most likely to have given to that supervisor, so sponsorship and giving can go together with no exchange between them: a gap beyond chance shows the two are associated, not that one bought the other, and here it rests on 5 sponsorships among 21 cases of giving, a thin basis. The counterparty is read from the title and matched by name, which can join two different firms. Contributions here are small beside the amounts because City law caps them. The amount in a file is not always money to the client: under a cost-sharing agreement, a lease of City property or a settlement the client may be the one paying, and some files set rules for a future competition instead of awarding anything. Who sponsors what, and who voted, are on the record; whether any of it was connected to the giving is not. For 332 roll calls the Clerk’s vote page says “by the following vote” and lists no member, 306 of them dated 2016-04-13 to 2016-07-26; 315 were read instead from the vote lines in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and 17 remain without member votes and are counted nowhere here. 2 files (160358, 160657) are left out wherever a final vote is counted or tested: for their last passage vote the vote page lists no member and the minutes print the action twice with different tallies, so it is not counted as unanimous and no earlier reading stands in for it. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).

San Francisco Ethics Commission: Campaign Finance - Transactions, all local committees (DataSF)
